title: It takes 23 minutes to refocus.
description:
It takes 23 minutes to refocus. The line is repeated everywhere, usually credited to Gloria Mark of UC Irvine.

An interview, not a paper. Gallup Business Journal, June 2006. A blogger who traced it in 2023 found the number in three interviews with Mark, and no printed paper containing it.

Resumed, not refocused. Mark told Gallup interrupted work was resumed on average in 23 minutes and 15 seconds, with about two other tasks in between.

Thirty six people. Three days. Mark said her team shadowed 36 managers, analysts, developers, engineers and project leaders. Gallup's page names no paper.

Average time before interrupted work was resumed, with other tasks first. Not a measured brain recovery time.

Interrupted people worked faster. In Mark's 2008 experiment they finished sooner but reported more stress, according to a blog and Silicon Canals. Neither page gives the sample size.

The number measures the detour. It was never a stopwatch on your brain.

Sources:
- https://news.gallup.com/businessjournal/23146/Too-Many-Interruptions-Work.aspx: read in full. Established the 8 June 2006 Gallup Business Journal interview in which Gloria Mark of UC Irvine said interrupted work was resumed on average in 23 minutes and 15 seconds, with about two intervening tasks, 81.9 percent resumed the same day, and that her team shadowed 36 managers, financial analysts, software developers, engineers and project leaders for three days. Names no paper.
- https://blog.oberien.de/2023/11/05/23-minutes-15-seconds.html: read in full. Established that a 2023 attempt to trace the figure found it in three interviews with Mark, found no primary printed source, and found that Mark's 2008 paper reports interrupted participants taking less time on the task with much higher stress and never mentions the number 23.
- https://siliconcanals.com/t-work-interruptions-23-minutes-275-pings-organisational-focus/: read in full. Established that the headline overstates its own body text, which says the figure covers resuming interrupted work and is not a laboratory measure of recovery, and that in a simulated office task interrupted people finished faster, with no loss of quality, but reported more stress, frustration, effort and time pressure.
